lines.translit: ud re-a-ta ud an ki-bi-ta ba-an-[dim2-ma-ba]

i18n.en: In those days, in those days when heaven and earth had been [fashioned each from the other];

notes.official:
The composition opens with the canonical Sumerian *once-upon-a-time* formula *ud re-a-ta* — literally 'from those days', the stock primordial-time opener of Sumerian mythological narrative. The triple-temporal opener of vv 1-3 (*ud re-a-ta* / *ĝi6 re-a-ta* / *mu re-a-ta*) — 'in those days / in those nights / in those years' — is editorially-deliberate, structurally invoking a *long-ago* register that Foster, Jacobsen, Black et al., and ETCSL all preserve as 'in those days'. The cross-corpus ANE *primordial-time-opener* type includes Akkadian *inūma* (*Enūma Eliš*: *enūma eliš lā nabû šamāmū* — 'when on high heaven had not been named') and Hebrew *be-reshit* (Gen 1:1) and *be-yom asot YHWH Elohim* (Gen 2:4b). See overlay entry `ud-re-a-ta-once-upon-a-time-formula`.

The phrase *an ki-bi-ta ba-an-dim2-ma-ba* is the Sumerian heaven-and-earth-separation cosmogonic-formula. The crux is the suffix *-bi-ta* on *ki* — '(from) its (counterpart)', the reciprocal-ablative. Modern scholarly consensus (Jacobsen *The Treasures of Darkness* 1976 pp. 167-168; Kramer *Sumerian Mythology*; Lambert *Babylonian Creation Myths* 2013 ch. 9) reads the line as naming a *creation-by-separation* cosmology: heaven and earth begin undifferentiated and are separated. The wider Sumerian-Akkadian separation-cosmogony tradition — *Enūma Eliš* IV.137-140 (Marduk splits Tiamat to make heaven and earth); *Gilgameš, Enkidu, and the Netherworld* prologue (lines 8-13, 'after heaven had been separated from earth'); *KAR* 4 — supports this reading. Cross-corpus to Gen 1:6-8 (the *raqia* separates waters from waters); see overlay entry `an-ki-bi-ta-heaven-and-earth-separation-cosmogony` and existing central entry `raqia`. Brackets [...] mark restored text per the ETCSL convention preserved by WoH: see overlay entry `lacuna-bracket-convention-sumerian-mesopotamian-project-standard`.

lines.cuneiform: 𒌓 𒊑𒀀𒋫 𒌓 𒀭 𒆠𒁉𒋫 𒁀𒀭𒁶𒈠𒁀

i18n.en: in those nights, in those nights when heaven and earth had [been fashioned each from the other];

notes.official: Second member of the triple-temporal opener (see commentary at v 1). The *ĝi6* (night) variant doubles the temporal opener of v 1; the parallel structure is a standard Sumerian poetic-rhetorical device. The *-bi-ta ba-an-dim2-ma-ba* construction recurs verbatim — the separation-cosmogony formula is doubled across vv 1-2. The /ba\ marker indicates the sign is damaged but securely-read; per the WoH convention this is silently collapsed in the prose (see overlay entry `lacuna-bracket-convention-sumerian-mesopotamian-project-standard`).

lines.cuneiform: 𒈪 𒊑𒀀𒋫 𒈪 𒀭 𒆠𒁉𒋫 𒁀𒀭𒁶𒈠𒁀

i18n.en: [in those] years, in the years when [destinies had been decreed];

notes.official: Third member of the triple-temporal opener. The line introduces the verbal-idiom *nam tar* — 'to cut a destiny / decree a fate' — the foundational Sumerian theological-conceptual-category that will saturate the composition. *Nam* (destiny / fate) combines with *tar* (to cut) in the metaphor of *cutting* a destiny: the divinatory-and-juridical sense of *tar* — to *cut* a decision, to *determine* by *separation*. See central entry `nam-sumerian-destiny-fate-cross-corpus` for the cross-corpus Sumerian-Akkadian sibling-cluster (Sumerian *nam* + the Akkadian *šīmtu* destiny-lexeme) and the partial-functional-cognate Hebrew *goral* (lot, portion; Lev 16:8-10; Josh 14-19; Ps 16:5; Prov 16:33).

lines.cuneiform: 𒈬 𒊑𒀀𒋫 𒈬 𒉆 𒁀𒋻𒊏𒁀

i18n.en: when the Anuna had been born;

notes.official: First occurrence of the collective-noun for the great gods: *a-nun-na* — *Anuna*. The Anuna are the senior-body of the Mesopotamian pantheon, presided over by An (sky-god), Enlil (storm-god of Nippur), and Enki (wisdom-god of the abzu). The Sumerian-source form *Anuna* is preserved per the ETCSL convention; the Akkadian-form *Anunnakū / Anunnaki* (with the variously-analyzed *-ki/-ke₄* suffix), widely-popularized in modern literature, is documented at the central entry `anuna-collective-of-great-gods-cross-corpus`. Cross-corpus to the wider ANE divine-assembly tradition: Hebrew *bnei Elohim* (Gen 6:1-4; Job 1:6, 2:1, 38:7; Ps 82:1); Ugaritic *pḫr ʾilm*; see existing central entry `bnei-elohim-yarinu` and `digir-sumerian-divine-lexeme-cross-corpus`. The DINGIR-determinative ^d (the cuneiform-classifier prefix on divine names) is preserved in the translit field and dropped in the i18n.en prose per the overlay convention `dingir-prefix-prose-drop-convention`. The damage-but-readable marker /\ around *nun* is silently collapsed.

lines.cuneiform: 𒉣𒈾𒆤𒉈 𒁀𒌅𒌓𒁕𒀀𒁀

i18n.en: when the mother-goddesses had been taken in marriage;

notes.official: The compound *ama-Inana* is read here as a class-noun for the mother-goddesses (the plural-collective rather than a proper-name 'Ama-Inana' or an Inana-epithet); see overlay entry `ama-inana-mother-goddesses-class-noun`. Modern Sumerologist consensus (Jacobsen *The Harps that Once* 1987 pp. 151-152; Kramer-Maier *Myths of Enki* 1989 pp. 32-33; Black et al. *Literature of Ancient Sumer* 2004 p. 215) supports the collective reading from the verb-agreements in vv 5-7 (taken-in-marriage, distributed, pregnant-and-giving-birth — all naturally collective). The sign-string *nam-NIR.PA* is preserved in capitals in the ETCSL composite because the cuneiform-to-Sumerian phonetic-reading is uncertain; the meaning is securely 'marriage'.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂼𒀭𒈹 𒉆𒂠 𒁀𒌇𒀀𒁀

i18n.en: when the mother-goddesses had been distributed throughout heaven and earth;

notes.official: The mother-goddesses are distributed *an ki-a* — 'throughout heaven and earth'. The collective-action confirms the class-reading at v 5 (see overlay entry `ama-inana-mother-goddesses-class-noun`).

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂼𒀭𒈹 𒀭 𒆠𒀀 𒁀𒆷𒀀𒁀

i18n.en: when the mother-goddesses, having […], had become pregnant and given birth;

notes.official: The lacuna […] preserves the ETCSL editorial-apparatus convention (see overlay entry `lacuna-bracket-convention-sumerian-mesopotamian-project-standard`). The verbs *peš* ('to be pregnant, thick, fat') and *tud* ('to give birth') saturate the line with female-fertility-and-birth vocabulary, consistent with the mother-goddesses-class reading at vv 5-6.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂼𒀭𒈹  𒁀𒀀𒄫 𒅇𒌅𒁕𒀀𒁀

lines.translit: diĝir kurum6-ma-bi A X X unu2^?-bi-še3 ba-ab-keše2-a->

i18n.en: when the food-rations of the gods, … …, had been bound to their dining-hall;

notes.official:
First major occurrence of *diĝir* — the Sumerian foundational divine-class lexeme; see the project's first Sumerian-source central entry `digir-sumerian-divine-lexeme-cross-corpus`, with bidirectional sibling-links to the existing Hebrew central entries `elohim-as-translation`, `el-shaddai`, and `anokhi-elohei-X-avikha-ancestral-god-formula`. The DINGIR-sign (𒀭) is itself an eight-pointed star — the cuneiform pictograph of *heaven / star / sky* — and functions both as common-noun ('a god') and as orthographic-determinative on divine names (the ^d prefix preserved in the translit field). The Sumerian *diĝir* is functionally-cognate with Akkadian *ilum* and Hebrew *el / Elohim*; the three lexemes form the project's first cross-language divine-class vocabulary-cluster.

*Kurum6* names *food-rations* — the daily-bread the gods are entitled to from the temple-economy. The line introduces the gods-as-laborers / rationed-workers framing that the composition will develop: the senior-gods have food-rations bound to their dining-hall (*unu2*), but they are also the ones bearing the toil at the canals (v 9). The cross-corpus link to *Atraḫasīs* I (the gods' rations and toil) is documented at central entry `du-lum-dullu-divine-toil-relieved-by-humans-cross-corpus`. The X X markers preserve illegible cuneiform signs per the lacuna convention.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭 𒉻𒈠𒁉 𒀀   𒁉𒂠 𒁀𒀊𒆟𒀀

lines.translit: diĝir šar2-šar2 kiĝ2-ĝa2 al-sug2-ge-eš diĝir tur-tur du2-lum im-il2-il2-e-ne

i18n.en: the senior gods stood overseeing the work, while the lesser gods bore the toil.

notes.official:
The senior-vs-junior god distinction is structurally-foundational. *Diĝir šar2-šar2* (lit. 'the numerous/great gods') = senior-gods; *diĝir tur-tur* (lit. 'the small gods') = lesser-gods. The distinction reflects the wider Mesopotamian theological-hierarchy: in *Atraḫasīs* I the *Anunnaki* (senior gods, Akkadian-form of the Sumerian Anuna; see central entry `anuna-collective-of-great-gods-cross-corpus`) preside while the *Igigi* (junior laboring gods) bear the toil, which leads them to revolt and motivates the human-creation. The Sumerian *Enki and Ninmah* version does not deploy the *Igigi* name but the same structural-logic is present: senior-gods supervise, junior-gods toil, and humans are created to relieve the junior-gods' burden.

*Du2-lum* is the foundational Sumerian divine-toil lexeme and the cognate of the Akkadian *dullu / dullum* — one of the few clear loanwords from Sumerian into Akkadian. The *du-lum / dullu* keyword is the central technical-term of the *humans-relieve-divine-toil* topos that runs through *Enki and Ninmah* and saturates *Atraḫasīs* Tablet I. See central entry `du-lum-dullu-divine-toil-relieved-by-humans-cross-corpus`, with cross-corpus thematic-link to Hebrew *avodah*, *sevel*, and *mas oved* (existing central entry `mas-oved-corvee-labor-institutional-vocabulary-cross-corpus`).

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭 𒊹𒊹 𒆥𒂷 𒀠𒁻𒄀𒌍 𒀭 𒌉𒌉 𒌅𒈝 𒅎𒅍𒅍𒂊𒉈

lines.translit: diĝir id2 im> dun-dun-u3-ne saḫar-bi ḫa-ra-li im-dub-dub-be2-ne

i18n.en: The gods were dredging the watercourses <of clay>, and were heaping up its earth at Harali.

notes.official:
First occurrence of the foundational human-creation substance: *im* — clay. The lesser-gods are dredging the *id2* (watercourses, canals) and heaping up the *saḫar* (earth, silt) at *Harali*. The dredging-and-heaping-of-clay is the canonical Mesopotamian image of corvée-labor in the wet-Mesopotamian-marshland; the same labor that humans will be created to take over.

*Im* is the Sumerian foundational clay lexeme — the substance of human-creation across the Sumerian-Akkadian-Hebrew creation traditions. The cross-corpus sibling-cluster spans Sumerian *im* / Akkadian *ṭiṭṭu* / Hebrew *afar* (dust; Gen 2:7) and *chomer* (clay; Job 10:9; Isa 64:8); see central entry `im-sumerian-clay-of-human-creation-cross-corpus`, with bidirectional sibling-links to the existing Hebrew central entries `adam-adamah` and `afar-va-efer-creatural-humility`. The Hebrew Joban verb *qaratz* ('nip off, pinch'; Job 33:6: *me-chomer qoratzti gam-ani* — 'from clay I was nipped off') is the lexical-and-functional cognate of the Sumerian *kir3-kir3* ('nip off', deployed at *Enki and Ninmah* v 32 of the SIG7-EN/SIG7-HI birth-goddesses pinching pieces from the abzu-clay).

*Harali* is preserved as a toponym; the location is uncertain — possibly a real geographic region in the western/southern Sumerian periphery associated with precious metals (Hallo 1987; Potts 1997 p. 165), possibly a mythic-cosmographic primordial-mound. See overlay entry `harali-mythic-toponym-source-of-clay`.

The ETCSL composite marker > after *im* and the editorial-supply *<of clay>* in the English are preserved per the overlay convention `lacuna-bracket-convention-sumerian-mesopotamian-project-standard`.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭 𒀀𒇉 𒅎 𒂄𒂄𒅇𒉈 𒁉 𒊏𒇷 𒅎𒁾𒁾𒁉𒉈

lines.translit: diĝir im ar3-ar3-re-ne zi-bi inim am3-ma-ĝar-re-ne

i18n.en: The gods, grinding the clay, kept complaining about this life.

notes.official:
**Line 11 is one of the most-discussed cruxes in Sumerian literature.** The Sumerian *zi-bi inim am3-ma-ĝar-re-ne* admits two principal readings with named-scholarship divided.

**(i) The complain-about-life reading** — ETCSL's English; Black et al. *Literature of Ancient Sumer* 2004. Parses *zi-bi inim ĝar* as the idiomatic 'place words about their life' = 'complain about life'. *Zi* governs the abstract sense 'life'; *inim ĝar* governs the sense 'voice grievance'. The reading fits the narrative-flow of vv 8-15 (the gods toil, then weep; the lament motivates Enki's intervention).

**(ii) The breath-into-clay creation-summary reading** — Jacobsen *The Harps that Once* 1987 p. 153; Lambert *Babylonian Creation Myths* 2013 pp. 330-345; Bottéro-Kramer *Lorsque les dieux faisaient l'homme* 1989 pp. 188-192; Foster *Before the Muses* 3rd ed. 2005 p. 156 (variable). Parses the same string as 'placed breath / life-word into it' (the clay): the gods, *grinding* the clay, *put breath/life-word into it* — a proleptic-summary of the human-creation that the rest of the composition will describe in detail. The reading takes *zi* in its physical sense 'breath' (the basic lexical-meaning; see central entry `zi-sumerian-breath-of-life-cross-corpus`) and *inim* as a creator-word ('the divine speech-act that animates'). The reading creates an exact-parallel with Gen 2:7's *va-yipach b-apav nishmat chayyim* ('and he breathed into his nostrils the breath of life') — made explicit by Lambert and Jacobsen.

The WoH translation **retains the Translator's surface 'kept complaining about this life'** (ETCSL reading) for the i18n.en text and **surfaces the breath-into-clay alternate reading here in commentary** with the Gen 2:7 cross-corpus parallel. The line is one of the corpus's clearest sites of *creator-breathes-life-into-clay* comparative-mythology; the cross-corpus link is documented at the central entry `zi-sumerian-breath-of-life-cross-corpus` with bidirectional sibling-link to the existing Hebrew central entry `neshamah-chayim`. See also overlay entry `zi-inim-line11-breath-into-clay-vs-complain-about-life-crux` for the philological detail.

i18n.en: At that time, the one of broad understanding, the maker, the one who brings into being all the senior gods —

notes.official: Enki's introductory-epithet-cluster: *ĝeštug2 daĝal* ('broad understanding, wide-of-ear'), *mud* ('the maker / creator'), and *ĝal2-ĝal2* ('the one who brings into being'). The *ĝeštug2 daĝal* epithet — literally 'wide ears' — names wisdom as a *capacity-for-listening*, characteristically Sumerian (the ear is the seat of wisdom in the Sumerian metaphorical-imagination). Enki's epithets across the composition emphasize his craftsmanship-and-wisdom function; see central entry `an-enlil-nudimmud-cosmic-triad-cross-corpus` on the *Nudimmud* epithet of Enki (vv 26, 47) and on the cosmic-triad An / Enlil / Enki-Nudimmud.

lines.cuneiform: 𒌓𒁀 𒄑𒌆𒉿 𒂼 𒄷𒄭 𒀭 𒊹𒊹 𒅅𒅅

lines.translit: ^den-ki-ke4 engur buru3 a-sur-ra ki diĝir na-me šag4-bi u6 nu-um-me

i18n.en: Enki, in the deep engur, in the flowing subterranean waters, the place into whose interior no god can peer in wonder —

notes.official:
Enki's cosmographic-domain: the *engur* (subterranean fresh waters) and the *a-sur-ra* (flowing subterranean waters). The lines deploy three closely-related Sumerian cosmographic-lexemes — *abzu* (v 31), *engur* (here), *a-sur-ra* (here) — for the subterranean fresh-water cosmos that is Enki's domain at Eridu. The three terms are not strictly synonymous: *abzu* names the cosmographic-region as a whole and as Enki's temple-domain; *engur* names the watery-mass itself; *a-sur-ra* names the flow or spring-water.

This is the foundational cross-corpus cosmographic-vocabulary cluster. The Sumerian-Akkadian-Hebrew sibling-cluster: *Sumerian abzu / engur / a-sur-ra* ↔ *Akkadian apsû* (loanword from Sumerian; personified in *Enūma Eliš* as Tiamat's husband) ↔ *Hebrew tehom* (cosmographic deep, demythologized from *Tiamat*; Gen 1:2; Gen 7:11; Ps 33:7) ↔ *Akkadian tiāmtu / Tiamat* (the salt-sea cosmos; the slain dragon-goddess in *Enūma Eliš*). The Heidel-Westermann-Tsumura *tehom-Tiamat* etymological-debate is documented at the central entry `abzu-engur-sumerian-subterranean-deep-cross-corpus`, with bidirectional sibling-link to the existing Hebrew central entry `tehom`.

The phrase *ki diĝir na-me šag4-bi u6 nu-um-me* — 'the place into whose interior no god can peer in wonder' — emphasizes Enki's abzu as a *primordial-secret-domain* inaccessible even to the other gods; the cosmographic-secrecy of Enki's domain is a recurring motif across the Enki-cycle.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒇉 𒌋 𒀀𒋩𒊏 𒆠 𒀭 𒈾𒈨 𒊮𒁉 𒅆𒂍 𒉡𒌝𒈨

i18n.en: was lying on his bed, sunk in sleep, and would not rise.

notes.official: Enki sleeps in his sleeping-quarter (*ki-nu2*) and does not rise. The image of the *sleeping-wise-god* who must be awakened to address a crisis is recurrent across the Mesopotamian Enki-and-Ea tradition; the awakening-by-mother (vv 17-24, where Namma carries the gods' tears to her son and rouses him) is the composition's narrative-pivot.

lines.cuneiform: 𒆠𒈿𒉌 𒉌𒈿 𒅇 𒆪 𒉡𒌝𒍣𒍣

lines.translit: diĝir er2-ra im-pad-pad-ne a-nir ĝal2 i3-ak im-me-ne

i18n.en: The gods broke into tears; they raised a lament, saying:

notes.official: The gods' lament. *Er2* (tears) and *a-nir* (lament) are paired lexemes saturating the composition's vv 15-23 lament-and-appeal section. Cross-corpus to *Atraḫasīs* I.300-340 (the gods' lament motivates Mami's deliberation and the human-creation) and to Gen 6:6 (the Yahwistic-source's *va-yinnachem YHWH... va-yitatzev el-libbo* — 'YHWH was grieved and pained in his heart'; existing central entry not yet on this; flagged for future).

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭 𒀀𒅆𒊏 𒅎𒉻𒉻𒉈 𒀀𒉪 𒅅 𒉌𒀝 𒅎𒈨𒉈

i18n.en: "As for him who lies sleeping there, <as for him> who does not rise from his bed —

notes.official: The gods' direct-speech complaint addressed to Namma about Enki's persistent sleep. The angle-bracket editorial-supply <as for him> is preserved per the overlay convention `lacuna-bracket-convention-sumerian-mesopotamian-project-standard`.

lines.cuneiform: 𒇽 𒆪𒊏 𒉌𒈿𒀀𒊏 𒆠𒈿𒁉 𒉡𒌝𒍣𒍣

i18n.en: Namma, the foremost mother who gave birth to all the senior gods,

notes.official: Namma is the Sumerian primordial mother-goddess — the *ama palil u3-tud diĝir šar2-šar2-ra-ke4-ne* ('foremost mother who gave birth to all the great gods'). She is the mother of Enki (addressed throughout the composition as *ama-ĝu10* — 'my mother') and is associated with the *abzu* (the subterranean fresh waters; v 31). The Namma-Tiamat cognate-debate is documented at the central entry `namma-primordial-mother-goddess-tiamat-comparandum`: older comparative-Sumerology (Jacobsen *The Treasures of Darkness* 1976 pp. 110-116; Lambert *Babylonian Creation Myths* 2013 ch. 9) often identified Sumerian *Namma* with Akkadian *Tiamat* as both being primordial-mother-deities associated with the cosmic-watery-deep; more recent scholarship (Wiggermann *RlA*) is more cautious — the functional parallel is strong but the etymological-cognate-status is not secure. The WoH translation does not pre-resolve the cognate-debate. The Sumerian-source form *Namma* is preserved (ETCSL standard); the older Anglophone form *Nammu* is documented in commentary.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒇉𒆤 𒂼 𒅆𒁺 𒅇𒌅 𒀭 𒊹𒊹𒊏𒆤𒉈

i18n.en: carried the tears of the gods to her son:

notes.official: Namma carries the gods' tears (*er2*) to her son Enki (*dumu-ni*). The maternal-intercession motif structures the narrative-pivot: the gods' direct-speech complaint to Namma (v 16) becomes Namma's appeal to Enki (vv 19-23).

lines.cuneiform: 𒀀𒅆𒊏 𒀭𒊑𒂊𒉈 𒌉𒉌𒅕 𒁀𒅆𒅔𒁺

i18n.en: "… are you really lying there asleep, and really lying down in sleep?

notes.official: Namma's opening rebuke. The X marks an illegible cuneiform sign per the lacuna convention.

lines.cuneiform: 𒈬𒌦𒅆𒈿𒅇𒉆 𒅇 𒈬𒌦𒅆𒆪𒆪𒈾𒉆

i18n.en: […] … … […], and [you do not] rise!

notes.official: Heavily-damaged line. The TE BA cuneiform sign-values are preserved in capitals where the reading is uncertain. The bracketed restorations follow ETCSL.

lines.cuneiform: 𒋼 𒁀  𒉡𒈬𒌦𒍣𒍣

lines.translit: dim3-me2-er šu dim2-dim2-ma-zu X gu2^?-bi im-tu10-tu10-ne

i18n.en: The gods, your handiwork — …, are striking down their (own) necks (in grief).

notes.official: *Dim3-me2-er* is a phonetic-variant spelling of *diĝir* (the Sumerian foundational divine-class lexeme; central entry `digir-sumerian-divine-lexeme-cross-corpus`); the variant spelling reflects a phonological-development in the Sumerian-lexicon and is widely-attested in Sumerian literary texts. The line names the gods as Enki's *handiwork* — *šu dim2-dim2-ma-zu* — emphasizing Enki's creator-function and motivating Namma's appeal: Enki, the maker of the gods, must intervene to relieve their distress.

lines.cuneiform: 𒈕𒈪𒅕 𒋗 𒁶𒁶𒈠𒍪  𒁉 𒅎𒄽𒄽𒉈

lines.translit: du5-mu-ĝu10 ki-nu2-zu zig3-ga [i-bi2] ma-al-la-zu-ta na-aĝ2-kug-zu u3-mu-e-kiĝ2-ĝa2

i18n.en: My son, rise from your bed; with the [eyes] that are at your disposal, with the wisdom that is yours, having sought out (a remedy) —

notes.official: Namma's appeal proper begins. The lexeme *na-aĝ2-kug-zu* — *wisdom* — is the Sumerian foundational wisdom-lexeme (parsing *nam* — abstract-class-noun marker + *kug* — pure, holy + *zu* — knowledge: 'the pure-knowing' / 'the abstract-class-of-pure-knowing'). The Hebrew comparandum *chokhmah* (wisdom; Prov 1-9; Job 28; widely-attested) names the same functional-conceptual category; Akkadian *nēmequ* (wisdom; in *Ludlul bel nemeqi* — 'I will praise the lord of wisdom', the Akkadian Job-of-Babylon) is the Akkadian-form. The cross-corpus wisdom-vocabulary cluster spans the Sumerian-Akkadian-Hebrew traditions and will be elaborated in subsequent Mesopotamian translations.

lines.cuneiform: 𒂅𒈬𒈬 𒆠𒈿𒍪 𒍣𒂵 𒄿𒉈 𒈠𒀠𒆷𒍪𒋫 𒈾𒉘𒆬𒍪 𒅇𒈬𒂊𒆥𒂷

i18n.en: fashion a substitute for the gods (?), so that they may be released from their toil!"

notes.official:
**The pivotal command in Namma's appeal: 'fashion X so that the gods may be released from their toil!'** The crux is the noun-phrase *kiĝ2-sig10 dim3-me2-er-e-ne-ke4*. ETCSL's token-gloss reads *kiĝ2-sig10* as 'late afternoon meal' — but the natural literal reading 'evening meal of the gods' makes poor narrative-sense (how would fashioning an evening meal release the gods from their toil?). Four scholarly reading-camps: **(i) the substitute-laborer reading** (Black et al. *Literature of Ancient Sumer* 2004; ETCSL English): a 'substitute' or 'replacement-worker' — humans — fashioned to take over divine toil. **(ii) Jacobsen's create-worker reading** (*The Harps that Once* 1987 p. 153): 'create work for the gods' or 'fashion the laborer for the gods' — a similar functional reading. **(iii) The literal evening-meal reading** (Foster *Before the Muses* 3rd ed. 2005 p. 156): retains the literal 'late-afternoon meal of the gods' and reads the verse as an obscure ritual-instruction. **(iv) The 'menial-work' reading** (Falkenstein and older Anglophone scholarship): paraphrastic 'do the daily-work for the gods'. The WoH adopts reading (i) — 'fashion a substitute for the gods (?)' — following Black et al. and ETCSL, with the (?) flag preserving the philological uncertainty. See overlay entry `kig-sig-line23-substitute-vs-evening-meal-crux`.

This is the composition's *humans-fashioned-to-relieve-divine-toil* command — the foundational cross-corpus motif documented at the central entry `du-lum-dullu-divine-toil-relieved-by-humans-cross-corpus`. The cross-corpus parallel at *Atraḫasīs* I.190-217 is direct: the senior-gods deliberate, the wise-god (Ea / Enki) intervenes, humans are created from clay to relieve the toil. Hebrew comparanda: *avodah*, *sevel*, and the *mas oved* corvée-labor institutional-vocabulary (existing central entry `mas-oved-corvee-labor-institutional-vocabulary-cross-corpus`).

lines.cuneiform: 𒆥𒋧 𒈕𒈪𒅕𒂊𒉈𒆤 𒅇𒈬𒂊𒁶 𒌅𒈝𒁉 𒁀𒌅𒇻𒉈

i18n.en: At the word of his mother Namma, Enki rose from his bed.

notes.official: The narrative-pivot: Namma's appeal succeeds; Enki rises. *Inim ama-na* — 'the word of his mother' — picks up the *inim* lexeme of v 11 (the *zi-bi inim ĝar* construction; see overlay entry `zi-inim-line11-breath-into-clay-vs-complain-about-life-crux`) and applies it now to maternal-speech-as-effective-call.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒅗 𒂼𒈾 𒀭𒇉𒆤 𒆠𒈿𒈾 𒁀𒋫𒍣

lines.translit: ḫal-an-kug niĝin2 šag4 kuš2-u3-da-na ḫaš im-mi-/ni\-[ra]

i18n.en: In Hal-anku, the chamber of his pondering, he slapped his thigh in his heart-weariness.

notes.official: *Hal-anku* (ḫal-an-kug; lit. 'pure division of heaven') is Enki's private deliberation-chamber within the abzu. The toponym is preserved per the convention for opaque Sumerian temple-names; see overlay entry `hal-anku-enki-deliberation-chamber`. The *thigh-slapping* gesture is a recurring Mesopotamian *deliberation-pondering* gesture, attested in royal-inscriptions and cult-texts.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒆬 𒆸 𒊮 𒊨𒅇𒁕𒈾  𒅎𒈪𒉌𒊏

lines.translit: ĝeštug2 ĝizzal en3 tar […] nam-kug-zu mud me-dim2 niĝ2-nam-ma SIG7-EN SIG7-ḪI im-ta-an-e3

i18n.en: The wise and discerning one, the deliberator […], the wisdom-bearer who brings into being the form of everything, brought forth the SIG7-EN and the SIG7-HI (the birth-goddesses?).

notes.official:
Enki, the *wisdom-bearer* who brings into being the *me-dim2* (form / articulation; see overlay entry on the lexeme below) of everything, *brings forth* the **SIG7-EN and SIG7-HI** — the team of birth-goddesses who will help Ninmah shape humans from the abzu-clay. The cuneiform sign-readings SIG7-EN and SIG7-HI are uncertain; ETCSL preserves them in capitals because no secure vocalization is established. Jacobsen reads 'Sigensigdu and Sigenshudu' (conjectural); Kramer-Maier read 'Imma-en and Imma-hi' under an alternative *imma*-vocalization. See overlay entry `sig7-en-sig7-hi-birth-goddesses-uncertain-vocalization`.

The lexeme *me-dim2* — 'form, articulation, limbs' — is one of the composition's recurring craftsman-vocabulary keywords; it covers both the abstract sense 'form' and the concrete sense 'limbs/body'. The lexeme recurs at vv 28, 32, 54, 83, 133.

lines.cuneiform: 𒄑𒌆𒉿 𒄑𒌆𒉿𒎓𒋡 𒇷 𒋻  𒉆𒆬𒍪 𒄷𒄭 𒈨𒁶 𒃻𒉆𒈠 𒅊𒂗 𒅊 𒅎𒋫𒀭𒌓𒁺

i18n.en: Enki set his hand to the task and turned his attention to it.

notes.official: Enki's preparation. *A2* ('arm, strength, side') and *ĝeštug2* ('ear, wisdom, attention') are the foundational Sumerian craftsmanship-and-wisdom lexemes; combining them names the *active-attention-and-skill* Enki brings to the human-creation task.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒀉𒉌 𒁀𒅆𒅔𒁺 𒄑𒌆𒉿 𒉌𒆸𒆸𒂊

lines.translit: ^den-ki-ke4 mud me-dim2 ni2-te-a-na šag4-bi ĝeštug2-ta u3-mu-ni-de5-ge

i18n.en: Enki, having drawn out from his own mind the form of his own being —

notes.official: Enki draws the *me-dim2 ni2-te-a-na* — 'the form of his own being' — from his own *šag4* ('heart, interior') and *ĝeštug2* ('ear, mind, wisdom'). The line introduces a strikingly self-referential creation-logic: Enki shapes the human after his own form, drawn from his own mind. The line is a strong cross-corpus parallel to Gen 1:26-27 (*na'aseh adam b-tzalmenu* — 'let us make adam in our image, after our likeness'); see existing central entry `elohim-as-translation` for the cross-corpus divine-self-reference at human-creation, and the planned future entry on Gen 1:26-27 *tzelem v-demut*.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒄷𒄭 𒈨𒁶 𒉎𒋼𒀀𒈾 𒊮𒁉 𒄑𒌆𒉿𒋫 𒅇𒈬𒉌𒊑𒄀

i18n.en: he addressed his mother Namma:

notes.official: Narrative-pivot to Enki's reply-speech. The maternal-address foregrounds Namma's role in the human-creation: she is not merely the messenger of the gods' tears but the formal-addressee of Enki's creation-instructions.

lines.cuneiform: 𒂼𒉌 𒀭𒇉𒊏 𒅗 𒈬𒌦𒈾𒌤𒂊

lines.translit: ama-ĝu10 mud mu-ĝar-ra-zu i3-ĝal2-la-am3 zub-sig3 diĝir-re-e-ne keše2-i3

i18n.en: "My mother, the creature whose name you have pronounced — it exists. Bind upon it the corvée-basket of the gods!

notes.official: Enki's instruction to Namma. *Zub-sig3* (Sumerian-lemma *dusu*; Akkadian *tupšikku*) is the **earth-carrying basket / corvée-labor-basket** — the iconic Mesopotamian symbol of the laborer's burden. The image is widely-attested across Mesopotamian iconography: the kudurru boundary-stones depict the king carrying the dusu on his head; the Ur-Nammu stele and the Gudea cylinders depict king-and-laborers carrying the basket. *Binding the corvée-basket upon the human-creature* is the iconographic-equivalent of *transferring-the-toil* from gods to humans. See central entry `zub-sig-dusu-corvee-basket-cross-corpus`, with cross-corpus link to Hebrew *sevel* (burden; Isa 9:3, 10:27, 14:25; Ps 81:7) and the wider Hebrew *avodah / sevel* labor-vocabulary cluster.

lines.cuneiform: 𒂼𒈬 𒄷𒄭 𒈬𒃻𒊏𒍪 𒉌𒅅𒆷𒀀𒀭 𒉺 𒀭𒊑𒂊𒉈 𒆟𒉌

i18n.en: When you have mixed the heart of the clay that is over the abzu —

notes.official:
**The abzu — Enki's subterranean fresh-water domain — and the clay that lies over it: the foundational cosmographic-and-material locus of human-creation.** Enki instructs Namma to mix the *im ugu abzu-ka* — 'the clay that is over the abzu', the wet-clay-mud at the cosmographic-boundary-zone between the subterranean fresh waters and the earth's surface. This is the specific material from which humans are crafted.

The cross-corpus link to Gen 2:7 is foundational: the Hebrew text has *va-yitzer YHWH Elohim et ha-adam afar min ha-adamah* ('and YHWH Elohim formed the human, dust from the ground'), with the immediately-preceding v 2:6 *v-ed yaaleh min ha-aretz v-hishqah et kol-pnei ha-adamah* ('and a mist / spring rose up from the earth and watered the whole face of the ground'). Both creation-stories locate the human-creation-substance at the boundary-zone between subterranean-water and earth-surface — the wet-clay-mud where deep-water and dry-ground meet. The conceptual-parallel is documented in **Westermann** *Genesis 1-11* (1984) and **Sparks** *Ancient Texts for the Study of the Hebrew Bible* (2005). See central entries `abzu-engur-sumerian-subterranean-deep-cross-corpus` and `im-sumerian-clay-of-human-creation-cross-corpus`, with bidirectional sibling-links to the existing Hebrew central entries `tehom`, `adam-adamah`, and `afar-va-efer-creatural-humility`.

lines.cuneiform: 𒊮 𒅎 𒌋𒅗 𒍪𒀊𒅗 𒅇𒈬𒂊𒉌𒅔𒊹

lines.translit: SIG7-EN SIG7-ḪI im mu-e-kir3-kir3-re-ne za-e me-dim2 u3-mu-e-ni-ĝal2

i18n.en: the SIG7-EN and SIG7-HI will nip off the clay (in pieces), and you (yourself) will give it form.

notes.official: The birth-goddesses (SIG7-EN and SIG7-HI; see overlay entry `sig7-en-sig7-hi-birth-goddesses-uncertain-vocalization`) **nip off** (*kir3-kir3*) pieces of the clay from the abzu-clay; Namma herself gives it form (*me-dim2 ĝal2*). The Sumerian verb *kir3-kir3* — 'to nip off, pinch off' — is the **lexical-and-functional cognate of Hebrew *qaratz*** at **Job 33:6**: *hen ani k-fikha la-El me-chomer qoratzti gam-ani* — 'behold, I am, as you are, before the El, from clay I was nipped off (= pinched out)'. This is one of the corpus's clearest **cross-corpus verb-cognates**: the same craftsman's-gesture of *pinching off pieces of clay* appears in both the Sumerian creation narrative and the Hebrew Joban poetry. See central entry `im-sumerian-clay-of-human-creation-cross-corpus` for the substance-and-verb cross-corpus cluster (Sumerian *im* + *kir3-kir3* ↔ Hebrew *chomer* + *qaratz*).

lines.cuneiform: 𒅊𒂗 𒅊 𒅎 𒈬𒂊𒆸𒆸𒊑𒉈 𒍝𒂊 𒈨𒁶 𒅇𒈬𒂊𒉌𒅅

i18n.en: Let Ninmah act as your assistant.

notes.official: First occurrence of the principal birth-goddess: *Ninmah* (lit. 'the great lady'). The Sumerian birth-goddess is named by multiple distinct epithets across the literature: **Ninmah** (this composition), **Nintud** ('the lady who gives birth'), **Ninhursaĝa** ('the lady of the foothills / holy mountain'), and **Mami** (the proto-name, the most archaic). All four epithets refer to the same chief-mother-goddess-and-birth-deity function. The Akkadian-form is *Bēlet-ilī* ('lady of the gods') or *Mami / Aruru*. See overlay entry `ninmah-ninhursaga-nintud-birth-goddess-epithet-cluster`. The WoH spelling *Ninmah* (with the digraph *h*) follows the anglicization convention `sumerian-proper-name-transliteration-convention`; the translit field preserves *Ninmaḫ* with the ḫ.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒎏𒂊 𒀭𒋫𒍪 𒀝𒂊

i18n.en: Ninimma, Shu-zi-ana, Ninmada, Ninbarag,

notes.official: First half of the seven (or eight, counting the doubled Ninbarag in the manuscript-variant) birth-assistant mother-goddesses who serve as Ninmah's midwives. The «&d;nin-barag» notation marks a scribal-addition the editor marks for deletion (the doubled <<word>> ETCSL marker). See overlay entry `eight-birth-assistant-goddesses-vv34-35`. The anglicized digraph forms *Shu-zi-ana* (not *Šu-zi-ana*) follow the WoH convention `sumerian-proper-name-transliteration-convention`.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒎏𒅊 𒀭𒋗𒍣𒀭𒈾 𒀭𒎏𒈠𒁕 𒀭𒎏𒁈

i18n.en: Ninmug, ShAR.ShAR.GABA, and Ninguna —

notes.official: Second half of the birth-goddess-list. *ShAR.ShAR.GABA* is preserved in capitals because the cuneiform sign-vocalization is uncertain (the cuneiform-determinative ^d preserves the divine-class-classification). See overlay entry `eight-birth-assistant-goddesses-vv34-35`.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒎏𒈮 𒀭 𒀭𒎏𒁯𒈾

i18n.en: let them stand by as your midwives at the birthing.

notes.official: The seven birth-goddesses are to stand by Namma at the *tud* (birth) as midwives. *Tud-tud* (the reduplicated form of *tud* 'to give birth') is the standard Sumerian birth-verb.

lines.cuneiform: 𒌅𒌅𒀀𒍪 𒊏𒁺𒁍𒉈

lines.translit: ama-ĝu10 za-e nam-bi u3-mu-e-tar ^dnin-maḫ zub-sig3-bi ḫe2-keše2

i18n.en: My mother, once you have decreed its destiny, let Ninmah bind the corvée-basket upon it. This — humankind — has been brought forth!"

notes.official: The climactic-creation instruction: Namma is to **decree the destiny** (*nam tar*) of the human-creature; Ninmah is to **bind the corvée-basket** (*zub-sig3 keše2*) upon it. The combined formula links the foundational Sumerian *nam tar* destiny-decreeing-idiom (central entry `nam-sumerian-destiny-fate-cross-corpus`) with the *zub-sig3 / dusu* corvée-labor-symbol (central entry `zub-sig-dusu-corvee-basket-cross-corpus`). The line is one of the composition's principal sites of *humans-fashioned-and-destinied-to-bear-divine-toil* (central entry `du-lum-dullu-divine-toil-relieved-by-humans-cross-corpus`).

lines.cuneiform: 𒂼𒈬 𒍝𒂊 𒉆𒁉 𒅇𒈬𒂊𒋻 𒀭𒎏 𒉺𒁉 𒆟

i18n.en: […] he established humankind […]

notes.official: First occurrence of the Sumerian foundational humankind-lexeme: *nam-lu2-ulu3* — humanity / humankind / the human-race. The compound parses as *nam* (abstract-class-noun marker) + *lu2* (person, man) + *ulu3* (man, people). See central entry `nam-lu2-ulu3-sumerian-humankind-cross-corpus`, with bidirectional sibling-link to the existing Hebrew central entry `adam-adamah`. Cross-corpus to Akkadian *amēlūtu* (humankind) — the cross-corpus-functional-cognate.

lines.cuneiform: 𒉌𒆕 𒉆𒇽𒍇

i18n.en: […] humankind […]

notes.official: Heavily-damaged line; *nam-lu2-ulu3* preserved (see central entry `nam-lu2-ulu3-sumerian-humankind-cross-corpus`).

lines.cuneiform: 𒉆𒇽𒍇 𒀀𒀭𒈠

i18n.en: […] … head by head, head […]

notes.official: *Saĝ-e saĝ* — 'head by head' — likely the distributive-counting formula for the numerous new-humans being established. Heavily damaged.

lines.cuneiform: 𒊕𒂊 𒊕 𒀀𒀭𒈠

i18n.en: "[…] is your creating; the dining-hall, your …-ing, this is what shall be!"

notes.official: The *unu6* (dining-hall) lexeme picks up the v 8 framing: the gods' food-rations-and-dining-hall are now linked to the human-creation. The creation is for the divine-banquet-economy.

lines.cuneiform: 𒁶𒍪 𒋼𒀊 𒊑𒍪 𒂵𒀀𒀀𒀭

i18n.en: […] he raised up the light over the … humankind […]

notes.official: *Ĝiš-nu11* — 'light, lamp, eye-of-the-sun' — the divine-light is raised over the new humankind. The Sumerian *light-raised-over-creation* motif resembles Gen 1:3-5 (the cosmic light at the threshold of creation) and Gen 1:14-19 (the luminaries; see existing central entries `meorot` and `hama-or-hagadol`).

lines.cuneiform: 𒊬𒂊 𒄑𒉢 𒈪𒉌𒅔𒅍 𒉆𒍇

lines.translit: […] sag2 numun2-e mi-ni-in-ri u3-tud na-bi mu-de5

i18n.en: […] he scattered the rushes, instructed the act of giving birth, gathered up its … (smoke?).

notes.official: Ritual-preparation for the human-creation: rushes (*numun2*) are scattered (used as bedding/marsh-material in Mesopotamian birth-rituals); the act of giving birth (*u3-tud*) is instructed; smoke (*na*) is gathered (incense-burning at the birth-rite). The Sumerian birth-ritual-vocabulary is well-documented (Stol *Birth in Babylonia and the Bible* 2000).

lines.cuneiform: 𒉺𒃶 𒍤𒆸𒂊 𒈪𒉌𒅔𒊑 𒅇𒌅 𒈾𒁉 𒈬𒊑

i18n.en: Enki, upon completing the entire round of the work, was glad in his heart.

notes.official: *Šag4-bi ba-ḫul2* — 'his heart was glad/joyful' — the creation-completion-joy formula. The closest cross-corpus parallel is **Gen 1:31** (*va-yar Elohim et kol-asher asah v-hineh tov me'od* — 'and Elohim saw all that he had made, and behold, it was very good'); the divine-satisfaction-at-creation-completion is a cross-corpus topos. See existing central entry `vayar-tov`.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒆥 𒆸𒆸𒁕  𒈪𒉌𒅔𒇲 𒊮𒁉 𒁀

i18n.en: For his mother Namma and for Ninmah he set out a banquet.

notes.official: The post-creation banquet — *ĝišbun* (cult-meal, ceremonial-banquet). The motif of *gods-banquet-after-creation* is the canonical Sumerian-Akkadian creation-closure: *Enūma Eliš* VI.69-79 has the great gods banqueting after Marduk's human-creation; *Atraḫasīs* I closes with a banquet-sequence. Cross-corpus to Hebrew Bible *creation-completion-and-sabbath* (Gen 1:31-2:3) — the closure-pattern is functionally-parallel though the Hebrew develops rest rather than banquet as the closing-motif.

lines.cuneiform: 𒂼𒉌 𒀭𒇉 𒀭𒎏𒂠 𒆠𒁉𒃻 𒈾𒀀𒀭𒈠𒉌𒅔𒃻

lines.translit: gu2 SIG7-EN SIG7-ḪI nun-ne-ke4 nam-tar gi saĝ ninda i-im-gu7-e

i18n.en: All the princely SIG7-EN and SIG7-HI ate of the destiny-loaves of the reed-head bread.

notes.official: The birth-goddesses join the banquet, eating the *nam-tar gi saĝ ninda* — the 'destiny-loaves of the reed-head bread', a ritual-bread-form associated with destiny-decreeing-rites. *Nam-tar* here in the abstract-destiny sense (see central entry `nam-sumerian-destiny-fate-cross-corpus`; not in the proper-name Namtar-demon sense, which appears only at v 71 — see overlay entry `namtar-disease-demon-vs-destiny-parsing-crux`).

lines.cuneiform: 𒄘 𒅊𒂗 𒅊 𒉣𒉈𒆤 𒉆𒋻 𒄀 𒊕 𒃻 𒄿𒅎𒅥𒂊

i18n.en: An, together with Enlil and lord Nudimmud, was roasting holy kids.

notes.official: **The Sumerian-Akkadian cosmic-triad: An (sky-god), Enlil (storm-god of Nippur), Nudimmud (epithet of Enki).** The three senior-gods join the post-creation banquet, roasting holy kids (*maš kug*) as ritual-meal. *Nudimmud* (^dnu-dim2-mud) is one of Enki's foundational epithets, meaning approximately 'the one who fashions / the begetter / the creator'; the epithet emphasizes Enki's craftsman-and-creator function. See central entry `an-enlil-nudimmud-cosmic-triad-cross-corpus`. The cross-corpus Akkadian-form *Anu / Enlil / Ea* triad is the Akkadian-side parallel; the Hebrew Bible's divine-council tradition (see existing central entries `bnei-elohim-yarinu`, `el-elyon`, `el-shaddai`) is the functional Hebrew-side parallel.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂊 𒀭𒂗𒆤𒁉 𒂗 𒀭𒉡𒁶𒄷𒄭𒂊 𒈦 𒆬 𒄿𒅎𒉈𒉈

i18n.en: All the senior gods were uttering praises.

notes.official: The senior-gods praise Enki at the banquet. *Ka tar* — 'to open the mouth (in praise)' — is the standard Sumerian praise-utterance verbal idiom; the related *za3-mi2* praise-noun appears at the composition's closing v 141 (see central entry `za-mi-doxological-praise-formula-sumerian-cross-corpus`).

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭 𒊹𒊹𒊏𒆤𒂊𒉈 𒅗 𒋻 𒄿𒅎𒋛𒅋𒇷𒉈

lines.translit: en ĝeštug2 daĝal-la a-ba-a ĝeštug2 i3-de5-ge

i18n.en: "O lord of broad understanding — who is wise enough to give you counsel?

notes.official: The gods' praise-speech begins. The *ĝeštug2 daĝal-la* — 'wide-of-ear, of broad understanding' — epithet of v 12 recurs here in the doxological address.

lines.cuneiform: 𒂗 𒄑𒌆𒉿 𒂼𒆷 𒀀𒁀𒀀 𒄑𒌆𒉿 𒉌𒊑𒄀

lines.translit: en gal ^den-ki-ke4 niĝ2 ak-ak-zu-še3 a-ba-a i3-sig10-ge

i18n.en: Great lord Enki — who can match the things you have done?

notes.official: Continued doxological praise. The *a-ba-a* — 'who?' — interrogative-pronoun frames Enki's incomparability.

lines.cuneiform: 𒂗 𒃲 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒃻 𒀝𒀝𒍪𒂠 𒀀𒁀𒀀 𒉌𒋧𒄀

lines.translit: a-a tud-da-gin7 me nam tar-tar-ra me za-e al-me-en-na

i18n.en: Like a father who has begotten (them), you are the one in whom rest the me and the decreeing of destinies — yes, the me are yours alone!"

notes.official:
**The flagship Sumerian-only theological-keyword: *me*.** The lexeme names the *divine offices / cosmic functions / archetypal cultural-patterns* — the powers and ordinances of the structured-cosmos. No clean Akkadian, Hebrew, or English cognate exists; the closest Akkadian comparandum is *parṣū* (rites, ordinances), but the Sumerian *me* has a cosmographic-scope and a *transferable-power* aspect (cf. *Inana and Enki*, the *me*-list-of-civilizational-offices) that *parṣū* lacks. See central entry `me-sumerian-divine-offices-cosmic-functions`. The lexeme is preserved untranslated as *me* in the WoH translation.

The line's structural-pivot: the gods identify Enki as the master of both the *me* (the cosmic-offices) and the *nam tar* (the destiny-decreeing) — both foundational Sumerian theological-categories. Cf. central entry `nam-sumerian-destiny-fate-cross-corpus`.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀀𒀀 𒌅𒁕𒁶 𒈨 𒉆 𒋻𒋻𒊏 𒈨 𒍝𒂊 𒀠𒈨𒂗𒈾

i18n.en: Enki and Ninmah went on drinking beer, and their hearts grew giddy with pleasure.

notes.official: The **drunken-contest setup**: Enki and Ninmah drink beer (*kaš*) and their hearts grow *ul* (swell with joy, become giddy). The motif of the *drunken-deliberation-leading-to-creation-contest* is editorially significant: the contest of vv 53-101 (Ninmah fashions defective creatures; Enki finds destinies for them; the contest reverses; Enki fashions Umul; Ninmah cannot match it) is conducted *under the influence*. The Sumerian motif parallels — at a comparative-mythology level — *Inana and Enki* (where Inana steals the me from a drunk Enki) and various ANE drunken-divine-decision motifs. The motif has no direct Hebrew Bible cross-corpus parallel (Hebrew Bible mythology does not develop *drunken-divine-decision* topoi); the closest Greek-tradition comparandum is the Hephaestus-and-Dionysus creating-creatures-while-drinking topos (mentioned in the editorial-intake at the Translator's draft).

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒀭𒎏𒂊 𒁉 𒅎𒅘𒅘𒉈 𒊮𒁉 𒌌 𒈬𒌦𒋼

i18n.en: Ninmah spoke to Enki:

notes.official: Speech-introduction; Ninmah's challenge opens.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒎏𒂊 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒊏 𒅗 𒈬𒈾𒌤𒂊

i18n.en: "As for the form of mankind — whether it turns out fair or ill is in (my) hands.

notes.official: Ninmah's challenge proper. *Me-dim2* (form, articulation; the recurring craftsman-lexeme of vv 26, 28, 32, 83, 133) of *na-aĝ2-lu2-ulu3* (humanity; see central entry `nam-lu2-ulu3-sumerian-humankind-cross-corpus`). Ninmah claims authority over whether the human-form turns out *sag9* (fair, good) or *ḫul* (bad, ill).

lines.cuneiform: 𒈨𒁶 𒈾𒉘𒇽𒍇𒋫 𒊷𒄀  𒈠𒀠𒆷𒀀𒄰

lines.translit: ki šag4 gi4-a-ĝu10 na-aĝ2-tar bi2-ib-sig10-ge bi2-ib-ḫul-e

i18n.en: According to whatever my heart prompts me, I can determine its destiny — for good or for ill."

notes.official: Ninmah claims the *na-aĝ2-tar* (destiny-decreeing; the abstract-noun form of the *nam tar* verbal-idiom; see central entry `nam-sumerian-destiny-fate-cross-corpus`). The challenge sets up the contest of vv 59-101.

lines.cuneiform: 𒆠 𒊮 𒄄𒀀𒈬 𒈾𒉘𒋻 𒉈𒅁𒋧𒄀 𒉈𒅁𒂊

i18n.en: Enki answered Ninmah:

notes.official: Speech-introduction; Enki accepts the contest.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒀭𒎏𒂊 𒈬𒈾𒉌𒅁𒄄𒄄

lines.translit: nam-tar šag4-ge de6-a-zu sag9-ge ḫul ma-al ga-am3-ši-ib2-la2

i18n.en: "The destiny that your heart has conceived, whether for good or for ill — I will counter-balance it."

notes.official: **Enki's contest-acceptance: 'I will counter-balance (*la2*) your destiny-decree.'** The verb *la2* — the contest-balance verb — recurs at the composition's closing v 132 (where Enki declares 'Ninmah, may your work be counter-balanced!'). The *la2* verbal-construction is contested: ETCSL reads 'undo'; Jacobsen reads 'counter-balance / match'; Foster preserves the literal 'hang in the balance'. The WoH adopts the **counter-balance reading** following Jacobsen and the narrative-context — the contest is one of *matching*, not *undoing*: Enki finds a *destiny-and-social-role* for each of Ninmah's six defective creatures rather than dismissing them. See overlay entry `la2-line132-ninmah-work-counterbalanced-vs-undone`.

lines.cuneiform: 𒉆𒋻 𒊮𒄀 𒁺𒀀𒍪 𒊷𒄀  𒈠𒀠 𒂵𒀀𒀭𒅆𒌈𒇲

i18n.en: Ninmah took clay from over the abzu into her hand.

notes.official: **The first round of the contest opens.** Ninmah takes *im ugu abzu* — clay from over the abzu — into her hand. The substance is the same as Enki's instruction at v 31 (see central entry `im-sumerian-clay-of-human-creation-cross-corpus`; the cross-corpus *human-from-clay* topos saturates the Sumerian-Akkadian-Hebrew creation traditions). The first round will produce the six defective creatures (vv 59-78).

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒎏𒂊 𒅎 𒌋𒅗 𒍪𒀊𒀀 𒋗𒉌 𒈬𒉌𒅔𒋾

lines.translit: lu2 gi šu šu2-šu2 sa2-sa2-de3 nu-gam lu2-u3 am3-ma-ni-in-dim2

i18n.en: First she fashioned a man whose hands were so weak that he could not bend them — a true human, but disabled.

notes.official: **The first defective creature: the weak-handed man.** The catalogue of vv 59-78 lists six (or seven, with manuscript variants) defective creatures Ninmah fashions; for each, Enki decrees a destiny and assigns a social-role. The catalogue is *aetiological*: it provides divine-origin-explanations for the social-roles of disabled, atypical, or unusual humans. The catalogue's editorial-stance is strikingly inclusive: the defectives are not rejected but *integrated* into society through divine-decreed destinies. See overlay entry `lu2-gi-sushuru-sasade-nugam-weak-handed-disabled`. The composition's catalogue is comparable to the medical-omen *šumma izbu* tradition (the monstrous-birth-omens) but reframes the defectives' fate from *disaster* to *integration*.

lines.cuneiform: 𒇽 𒄀 𒋗 𒋙𒋙 𒁲𒁲𒉈 𒉡𒃵 𒇽𒅇 𒀀𒀭𒈠𒉌𒅔𒁶

lines.translit: ^den-ki-ke4 lu2 gi šu šu2-šu2 sa2-sa2-de3 nu-gam igi du8-a-ni-ta

i18n.en: When Enki saw the man whose hands were so weak that he could not bend them,

notes.official: Enki's response-formula. The catalogue follows a strict pattern: Ninmah fashions → Enki sees → Enki decrees destiny.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒇽 𒄀 𒋗 𒋙𒋙 𒁲𒁲𒉈 𒉡𒃵 𒅆 𒂃𒀀𒉌𒋫

i18n.en: he decreed his destiny: he set him to stand at the head of the king (as his attendant).

notes.official: The first destiny: the weak-handed man is *integrated as the king's attendant* — a court-position that does not require manual-labor. The aetiology explains the social-existence of palace-attendants who do not work with their hands; the disability is given divine-origin-and-purpose.

lines.cuneiform: 𒉆𒁉 𒄿𒉌𒅔𒋻 𒊕 𒈗𒆷𒆤 𒀀𒀭𒈠𒉌𒅔𒁺

lines.translit: gi4-bi ĝiš-nu11 gi4-gi4 lu2 u6-e am3-ma-ni-in-dim2

i18n.en: Secondly, she fashioned one who turned back the light — a blind man, the marvel of onlookers.

notes.official: **The second defective creature: the blind man.** The Sumerian *ĝiš-nu11 gi4-gi4* — 'turns back the light' — is the consensus reading for a blind man; the eyes 'turn back the light' rather than receiving it. See overlay entry `gi-nu-gi-blind-man-marvel-of-onlookers`.

lines.cuneiform: 𒄄𒁉 𒄑𒉢 𒄄𒄄 𒇽 𒅆𒂍𒂊 𒀀𒀭𒈠𒉌𒅔𒁶

i18n.en: When Enki [saw] the one who turned back the light, the marvel of onlookers,

notes.official: Enki's response.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒄑𒉢 𒄄𒄄 𒇽 𒅆𒂍𒂊 𒅆 𒂃𒀀𒉌𒋫

i18n.en: he decreed his destiny: he allotted to him the art of music.

notes.official: **The blind-musician aetiology.** *Nam-nar* — 'the art of music; the office of the *nar*' (Sumerian for *musician*; Akkadian *nāru*) — is allotted to the blind man. The blind-musician profession is widely-attested in Mesopotamian (and wider ANE / Greek) tradition: Homer's Demodokos in *Odyssey* 8; the blind Greek prophets Teiresias and Phineus; the rabbinic tradition of blind-men-gifted-in-song. See **Anne Kilmer** *RlA* s.v. *Musik*. The aetiology integrates blindness into society through a culturally-valued profession.

lines.cuneiform: 𒉆𒁉 𒄿𒉌𒅔𒋻 𒉆𒈜 𒈪𒉌𒅔𒁀

i18n.en: He set him to stand before the king as a great […] of the throne-dais.

notes.official: *Ušumgal* (lit. 'great serpent / dragon') is the Sumerian-Akkadian honorific-metaphorical lexeme for *pre-eminent one* / *lord* / *champion*; widely-applied to Marduk, Ningirsu, kings, and high-officials. The line is partly damaged; the specific role-noun is in the lacuna. See overlay entry `ushumgal-great-one-throne-dais`.

lines.cuneiform: 𒃲 𒃲𒁔𒆷 𒅆 𒈗𒆷𒆤 𒀀𒀭𒈠𒉌𒅔𒁺

lines.translit: {peš-bi [ĝiri3 2] ḫum ĝiri3 dab5-ba-a [am3-ma-ni-in-dim2]} {() [lu2] peš-bi ^lu2lil u3-tud-bi lu2-u3 am3-ma-[…]}

i18n.en: Thirdly, she fashioned one whose [two feet] were broken, a foot-bound man — {alternate manuscript: as her third [man] she fashioned a fool, the engendering of a (mere) human …}.

notes.official: **The third defective creature** — and the composition's first manuscript-variant. The main reading: a foot-bound man (broken feet, perhaps shackled). The alternate-manuscript reading: a *lu2lil* — a fool, with the further epithet *u3-tud-bi lu2-u3* ('its begetting was [merely] human' = the fool is begotten of ordinary human-procreation rather than divine-formation). Both readings preserved per the manuscript-variant-inline-rendering convention (see overlay entries `manuscript-variant-inline-rendering-convention` and `lu2lil-fool-court-defective-creature`).

lines.cuneiform: 𒄫𒁉 𒄊   𒄊 𒆪𒁀𒀀 𒀀𒀭𒈠𒉌𒅔𒁶  𒇽 𒄫𒁉 𒇽𒇸 𒅇𒌅𒁉 𒇽𒅇 𒀀𒀭𒈠

lines.translit: {^den-[ki-ke4] ĝiri3 2^! ḫum ĝiri3 dab5-ba igi [du8-a-ni-ta]} {() ^den-ki-ke4 ^lu2lil u3-tud-bi lu2-u3 igi du8-a-ni-/ta\}

i18n.en: When [Enki] saw the one with his two feet broken, the foot-bound — {alternate manuscript: when Enki saw the fool, the engendering of a (mere) human} —

notes.official: Both manuscript variants preserved (see overlay entry `manuscript-variant-inline-rendering-convention`).

lines.cuneiform: 𒆠𒆤 𒄊   𒄊 𒆪𒁀 𒅆 𒂃𒀀𒉌𒋫  𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒇽𒇸 𒅇𒌅𒁉 𒇽𒅇 𒅆 𒂃𒀀𒉌𒋫

lines.translit: {kiĝ2 […] kug-babbar-dim2 me-lem4-ma-ni /am3\-[ma]-ni-in-[X]} {() nam-bi i-ni-/in-tar\ saĝ lugal-la-ke4 im-ma-ši-in-gub}

i18n.en: {he … the work of a silversmith, his radiance …} {alternate manuscript: he decreed its destiny — he set him to stand at the head of the king}.

notes.official: Variant destinies. The first variant assigns the silversmith craft; the second assigns the king's attendant role (same as v 61 for the weak-handed man). The variants reflect different recensional traditions for the third defective's social-role.

lines.cuneiform: 𒆥  𒆬𒌓𒁶 𒈨𒉈𒈠𒉌 𒀀𒀭𒈠𒉌𒅔  𒉆𒁉 𒄿𒉌𒅔𒋻 𒊕 𒈗𒆷𒆤 𒅎𒈠𒅆𒅔𒁺

i18n.en: Fourthly, she fashioned a man who dripped water continually.

notes.official: **The fourth defective creature: the water-dripping man** — a man suffering from a urinary or excretory disorder (incontinence). The Sumerian medical-vocabulary (Stol *Birth in Babylonia and the Bible* 2000) attests this category.

lines.cuneiform: 𒄫𒄀 𒇽 𒀀 𒋩𒋩𒊏 𒀀𒀭𒈠𒉌𒁶

i18n.en: When Enki saw the man who dripped water continually,

notes.official: Enki's response.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒇽 𒀀 𒋩𒋩𒊏 𒅆 𒂃𒀀𒉌𒋫

lines.translit: a mu7-mu7 mi-ni-in-tu5 nam-tar su-bi am3-ma-ni-in-zig3

i18n.en: he bathed him with incantation-water and drove the namtar-demon out of his flesh.

notes.official: **The unique-in-this-composition disease-demon Namtar.** The Sumerian string *nam-tar* appears in the composition in the abstract-destiny sense at vv 3, 37, 46, 51, 55, 57, 78, 105, 107 (where it is the foundational divine-action verb); at **v 71 uniquely** it appears in the proper-name sense: *Namtar* the disease-demon, associated with plague and untimely death. Enki bathes the water-dripping man with *a mu7-mu7* (incantation-water; ritual-purification) and *drives the namtar-demon out of his flesh* — a healing-exorcism. See overlay entry `namtar-disease-demon-vs-destiny-parsing-crux` for the dual-parsing convention. Cross-corpus to the wider Mesopotamian disease-demonology: *Lamaštu*, *Pazuzu*, *Asakku*, *Sebettu* (the seven evil winds); see **Wiggermann** *Mesopotamian Protective Spirits* 1992.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀀 𒅲𒅲 𒈪𒉌𒅔𒋗𒉀 𒉆𒋻 𒋢𒁉 𒀀𒀭𒈠𒉌𒅔𒍣

i18n.en: Fifthly, she fashioned a woman who could not give birth.

notes.official: **The fifth defective creature: the woman who cannot give birth.** *Munus nu-u3-tud* — 'woman who does-not give birth' — the infertile-woman category. Infertility is a recurring biblical theme (Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah; cross-corpus to the patriarchal-matriarchs-infertility narratives). The Sumerian aetiology gives the infertile-woman a *productive social-role* rather than treating infertility as a curse.

lines.cuneiform: 𒄫𒄫𒄀 𒊩 𒉡𒅇𒌅 𒀀𒀭𒈠𒉌𒅔𒁶

i18n.en: When Enki saw the woman who could not give birth,

notes.official: Enki's response.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒊩 𒉡𒅇𒌅 𒅆 𒂃𒀀𒉌𒋫

lines.translit: {nam-bi /mi\-ni-in-tar e2-mi2-a-ke4 am3-ma-ni-in-du3} {() uš-bar mu-ni-in-du8 e2-mi2-a-kam am3-ma-ši-in-dim2}

i18n.en: {he decreed her destiny: he established her in the women's quarters} {alternate manuscript: he set her up as a weaver, made her a thing of the women's quarters}.

notes.official: **Variant destinies for the infertile woman**: established in the women's quarters (the first reading; *e2-mi2* — 'the house of the women / female-quarters'); set up as a weaver (*uš-bar* — weaver; the second reading). The aetiologies integrate infertility through productive-social-roles in the temple-and-palace women's economy. See manuscript-variant convention `manuscript-variant-inline-rendering-convention`.

lines.cuneiform: 𒉆𒁉 𒈪𒉌𒅔𒋻 𒂍𒊩𒀀𒆤 𒀀𒀭𒈠𒉌𒅔𒆕  𒍑𒁇 𒈬𒉌𒅔𒂃 𒂍𒊩𒀀𒄰 𒀀𒀭𒈠𒅆𒅔𒁶

lines.translit: peš-bal-gi lu2 su-ba ĝiš3 nu-ĝar gal4-la nu-ĝar am3-ma-ni-dim2

i18n.en: Sixthly, she fashioned a being whose body had been formed with neither penis nor vulva.

notes.official: **The sixth defective creature: the genitally-atypical individual** — fashioned with neither *ĝiš3* (penis) nor *gal4-la* (vulva). The explicit anatomical-vocabulary is securely-attested in the Sumerian medical-and-literary corpus. See overlay entry `lu2-su-ba-gish-galla-no-genitalia`.

lines.cuneiform: 𒄫𒁄𒄀 𒇽 𒋢𒁀 𒍑 𒉡𒃻 𒊩𒆷 𒉡𒃻 𒀀𒀭𒈠𒉌𒁶

lines.translit: ^den-ki-ke4 lu2 su-ba ĝiš3 nu-ĝar gal4-la nu-ĝar igi du8-a-ni-ta

i18n.en: When Enki saw the being whose body had been formed with neither penis nor vulva,

notes.official: Enki's response.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒇽 𒋢𒁀 𒍑 𒉡𒃻 𒊩𒆷 𒉡𒃻 𒅆 𒂃𒀀𒉌𒋫

i18n.en: he gave him the name "Eunuch (tiru) of Nibru",

notes.official:
**Naming the genitally-atypical individual as the *tiru* — the third-gender palace-and-temple courtier — of *Nibru* (Sumerian-source form of the Nippur toponym).** The Sumerian-Akkadian *tiru / girseqû* is a documented third-gender palace-and-temple role; see overlay entry `tiru-third-gender-courtier-palace-attendant`. The wider Mesopotamian third-gender cult-vocabulary includes the *kurgarra*, *assinnu*, and *galaturra* (male-bodied ritual-performers in Inana's cult); the Hebrew comparandum *saris* (eunuch; 2 Kgs 9:32; Esth 1:10; Isa 56:3-5; Matt 19:12) is functionally-parallel but not philologically-cognate.

*Nibru* is the Sumerian-source form; the Anglicized *Nippur* derives via Akkadian and Greek. See central entry `nibru-nippur-cuneiform-cross-corpus`. Nippur is the religious-and-political center of Sumer, the cult-city of Enlil and the location of the E-kur temple (see central entry `ekur-house-of-the-mountain-enlil-temple-cross-corpus`).

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭 𒂊 𒈬𒂊 𒈬𒉌𒅔𒄷𒈿𒀀

i18n.en: and decreed for him as his destiny to stand before the king.

notes.official: The *tiru* is given the destiny of standing before the king as palace-attendant. The aetiology integrates the genitally-atypical individual into the palace-and-temple society as a culturally-recognized role.

lines.cuneiform: 𒅆 𒈗𒆷𒆤 𒁺𒁍𒉈 𒉆𒁉 𒀀𒈠𒉌𒅔𒋻

lines.translit: {^dnin-maḫ-e im niĝin2 šu-na ki-a mu-un-šub lul-aš lib mu-un-ĝar} {() ^den-ki-ke4 im šu-niĝin2-na ki-a in-šub lul-aš i3-ni-gi}

i18n.en: {Ninmah cast aside the clay in her hand onto the ground; she fell into a dread silence} {alternate manuscript: Enki cast aside the whole of the clay in his hand onto the ground; … in dread silence}.

notes.official: **The first-round closure.** Ninmah (or Enki, in the variant) casts aside the remaining clay; the *lul-aš lib* — *dread silence / awe-silence* — closes the first round. The closure is editorially-significant: Ninmah has presented six defective creatures; Enki has found destinies for all six. The contest enters its second round with Enki's challenge (vv 80-83). See overlay entry `manuscript-variant-inline-rendering-convention`.

lines.cuneiform: 𒂊 𒅎 𒆸 𒋗𒈾 𒆠𒀀 𒈬𒌦𒊒 𒈜𒀸 𒈜 𒈬𒌦𒃻  𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒅎 𒋗𒆸𒈾 𒆠𒀀 𒅔𒊒 𒈜𒀸 𒉌𒉌𒄀

i18n.en: Great lord Enki then spoke to Ninmah:

notes.official: Speech-introduction; Enki's challenge opens.

lines.cuneiform: 𒂗 𒃲 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒀭𒎏𒀀𒊏 𒅗 𒈬𒌦𒈾𒌤𒂊

lines.translit: lu2 šu dim2-ma-zu-še3 nam-bi i-ni-in-tar ninda i-ni-in-šum2

i18n.en: "For the beings of your fashioning I have decreed destinies; I have given them their bread.

notes.official: Enki summarizes his contest-action: destinies decreed (*nam tar*), bread (*ninda*) given. The *bread-given* element is editorially-significant: each of Ninmah's six defectives receives not just a destiny-decree but a *bread-ration* — entry into the temple-economy. The defectives are fully-integrated, with the bread-ration as the institutional-marker of integration.

lines.cuneiform: 𒇽 𒋗 𒁶𒈠𒍪𒂠 𒉆𒁉 𒄿𒉌𒅔𒋻 𒃻 𒄿𒉌𒅔𒋧

lines.translit: ĝe26-e ga-na ga-mu-ra-ab-dim2 za-e u3-tud-bi nam-bi tar-ra-ab

i18n.en: Now then — let me, in turn, fashion (one) for you; you decree the destiny of the one I bring forth."

notes.official: The contest-reversal: now Enki will fashion, and Ninmah will decree the destiny. The reversal sets up the contest's climactic-act — the fashioning of Umul.

lines.cuneiform: 𒂷𒂊 𒂵𒈾 𒂵𒈬𒊏𒀊𒁶 𒍝𒂊 𒅇𒌅𒁉 𒉆𒁉 𒋻𒊏𒀊

lines.translit: ^den-ki-ke4 me-dim2 saĝ-ĝa2 X-ga^? ka šag4-ba a-ma-ni-dim2

i18n.en: Enki fashioned the form of the head, the …, the mouth, in its heart (= in the womb).

notes.official: Enki begins his fashioning. *Me-dim2* (form, articulation) and *saĝ* (head) and *ka* (mouth) are the body-part lexemes of the craftsman-fashioning. *In its heart* (*šag4-ba*) here in the *in-the-womb* sense — the fashioning takes place in the womb of the woman who will bear Umul (vv 85-87).

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒈨𒁶 𒊕𒂷  𒅗 𒊮𒁀 𒀀𒈠𒉌𒁶

i18n.en: He said to Ninmah:

notes.official: Speech-introduction.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒎏𒀀𒊏 𒅗 𒈬𒌦𒈾𒌤𒂊

lines.translit: {a ĝiš3 ak šag4 munus-a-ka ri-a} {() a gan šag4 munus-a-ka} a šag4-ga-na munus-bi mu-un-u3-tud

i18n.en: {"The seed of a penis acted in the womb of a woman} {alternate manuscript: the child-bearing water in the womb of a woman}: in her womb, that woman has given birth to it."

notes.official: Two manuscript variants describing the conception. Both describe the *biological-procreation* path (not the *clay-fashioning* path) for Umul's birth — Enki's contest-creation is born of a woman, not pinched from abzu-clay. The shift is editorially-significant: Enki's contest-creature is *more-uncanny* than Ninmah's — born of biological-conception yet so disabled that he is *neither living nor dead* (v 101).

lines.cuneiform: 𒀀 𒍑 𒀝 𒊮 𒊩𒀀𒅗 𒊑𒀀  𒀀 𒃶 𒊮 𒊩𒀀𒅗 𒀀 𒊮𒂵𒈾 𒊩𒁉 𒈬𒌦𒅇𒌅

i18n.en: Ninmah […] stood by for its birth.

notes.official: Ninmah, the chief birth-goddess, stands by for the birth — even of Enki's contest-creature. The cross-cooperation persists.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒎏  𒅇𒌅𒁉𒂠 𒀀𒀭𒈪𒉌𒁺

lines.translit: munus-bi ud-bi […] GA AŠ X KA {šag4-ba i-in-šub} {() saĝ-bi-iš [ba]-/ra\-an-e3}

i18n.en: That woman, on that day […] … … {it fell forth from her womb} {alternate manuscript: it came forth head-first}.

notes.official: Two manuscript variants describing the birth. Both describe an unusual-or-difficult delivery, prefiguring Umul's catastrophic disability.

lines.cuneiform: 𒊩𒁉 𒌓𒁉  𒂵 𒀸  𒅗 𒊮𒁀 𒄿𒅔𒊒  𒊕𒁉𒅖 𒁀𒊏𒀭𒌓𒁺

lines.translit: gi4-bi u4-mu-ul a-za-ad-bi gig-ga ki nam-X-bi gig-ga igi-bi gig-ga gu2-bi gig-ga

i18n.en: This second one was Umul: its head was sick, its place of …-ing was sick, its eyes were sick, its neck was sick.

notes.official:
**Umul: Enki's contest-creature.** Vv 88-91 list Umul's comprehensive disabilities. The etymology of *u4-mu-ul* is debated: Jacobsen reads 'my day is distant' (= short-lived); Black et al. read 'sickly-newborn' (a class-noun); ETCSL preserves as proper-name. See overlay entry `umul-sickly-creature-name-etymology`.

*A-za-ad* — a body-part lexeme of uncertain precise reference; the standard reading is 'head'; some scholars (Stol *Birth in Babylonia and the Bible* 2000) suggest 'fontanel' (the unossified soft-spot of a newborn's skull) in birth-and-defect contexts. See overlay entry `a-za-ad-head-fontanel-body-part`.

The catalogue of disabilities is so comprehensive that Umul is virtually a *catalogue-of-everything-wrong*. The Mesopotamian *šumma izbu* monstrous-birth-omen-tradition is the comparative-literature-genre to which Umul belongs; see **Lambert** 'A New Look at the Babylonian Background of Genesis' *JTS* 16 (1965); **Kilmer** 'Of Babies, Boats, and Arks' (1989).

lines.cuneiform: 𒄄𒁉 𒌓𒈬𒌌 𒀀𒍝𒀜𒁉 𒍼𒂵 𒆠 𒉆𒁉 𒍼𒂵 𒅆𒁉 𒍼𒂵 𒄘𒁉 𒍼𒂵

lines.translit: zi til-til ti sur-sur mur gig-ga šag4 gig-ga lipiš gig-ga

i18n.en: Its breath was failing, its ribs dripping, its lungs sick, its heart sick, its inner body sick.

notes.official: The disability-catalogue continues. *Zi til-til* — 'breath failing/ending' — picks up the *zi* lexeme of the v 11 crux (the breath-into-clay vs complain-about-life debate; see overlay entry `zi-inim-line11-breath-into-clay-vs-complain-about-life-crux` and central entry `zi-sumerian-breath-of-life-cross-corpus`). Where the gods at v 11 placed breath into the clay (on the Lambert-Jacobsen reading), Umul's *breath* is failing — the same lexeme, now in the dying-out sense rather than the animating sense.

lines.cuneiform: 𒍣 𒌀𒌀 𒋾 𒋩𒋩 𒄯 𒍼𒂵 𒊮 𒍼𒂵 𒀚 𒍼𒂵

lines.translit: šu-bi(source: NI) a-za-ad la2-la2 ka-bi-še3 ninda nu-ĝar murgu2 [saĝ]-du ze2-re

i18n.en: Its hand hung limp at its head; it could not lift bread to its mouth; its back and [skull] were broken.

notes.official: The disability-catalogue's most-disabling element: Umul cannot lift bread to his mouth. Bread (*ninda*) is the institutional-marker of integration into the temple-economy (cf. v 81 — Enki gave bread to each of Ninmah's defectives); Umul cannot eat the bread. The exclusion-from-the-bread-economy is editorially-foundational: it is what makes Umul *neither living nor dead* (v 101).

lines.cuneiform: 𒋗 𒉌 𒀀𒍝𒀜 𒇲𒇲 𒅗𒁉𒂠 𒃻 𒉡𒃻 𒈱 𒊕𒁺 𒍢𒊑

lines.translit: zag-še sur ĝiri3 sur-sur a-gar3 nu-DU am3-ma-ni-/in\-dim2

i18n.en: Its shoulder and feet trembled (?); it could not walk in the meadow — such a one he had fashioned.

notes.official: Closure of the disability-catalogue. Umul cannot walk *a-gar3* (in the meadow, in the open fields) — exclusion from agricultural-and-civic life.

lines.cuneiform: 𒍠𒊺 𒋩 𒄊 𒋩𒋩 𒀀𒃼 𒉡𒁺 𒀀𒀭𒈠𒉌𒅔𒁶

i18n.en: Enki said to Ninmah:

notes.official: Speech-introduction; Enki challenges Ninmah to decree Umul's destiny.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒀭𒎏𒊏 𒅗 𒈬𒈾𒌤𒂊

lines.translit: lu2 šu dim2-ma-zu nam i-ni-in-tar ninda mi-ni-[šum2]

i18n.en: "For the beings of your fashioning I decreed destinies; I [gave them] bread.

notes.official: Enki recapitulates his contest-action: destinies decreed, bread given.

lines.cuneiform: 𒇽 𒋗 𒁶𒈠𒍪 𒉆 𒄿𒉌𒅔𒋻 𒃻 𒈪𒉌𒋧

lines.translit: za-e lu2 šu dim2-ĝu10-uš nam-bi tar-ra-ab ninda ḫe2-[…-šum2]

i18n.en: Now you, in turn, decree the destiny of the being of my fashioning; let it [be given] bread!"

notes.official: The challenge proper: Ninmah is to decree Umul's destiny and give him bread.

lines.cuneiform: 𒍝𒂊 𒇽 𒋗 𒁶𒈬𒍑 𒉆𒁉 𒋻𒊏𒀊 𒃻 𒋧

i18n.en: When Ninmah [saw] Umul, she turned to [him].

notes.official: Ninmah's response begins. She approaches Umul, follows the established pattern (Ninmah-fashions → Enki-sees → Enki-decrees in round one, here in reverse).

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒎏𒂊 𒌓𒈬𒌌 𒅆 𒂃𒀀𒉌𒋫 𒂊𒉈𒂠 𒁀𒂊𒄄

lines.translit: u4-mu-ul mu-na-te en3 mu-na-tar-tar-re dug4-ga nu-zu-e

i18n.en: She drew near to Umul, kept questioning him — but he could not speak.

notes.official: Umul cannot speak. The exclusion from speech is exclusion from social-and-civic life; in the Sumerian aetiological-tradition, speech is foundational for participation in *kalam* (the Land; see central entry `kalam-ka-na-ag-the-land-cross-corpus`).

lines.cuneiform: 𒌓𒈬𒌌 𒈬𒈾𒋼 𒇷 𒈬𒈾𒋻𒋻𒊑 𒅗𒂵 𒉡𒍪𒂊

i18n.en: She brought him bread to eat — but he could not stretch out his hand for it.

notes.official: Ninmah attempts the bread-integration test (the same that worked for all six of her defectives); Umul fails. The cumulative-failure of Ninmah's tests prepares her concession at v 101.

lines.cuneiform: 𒃻 𒅥𒀀𒉌𒂠 𒈬𒈾𒀊𒁺 𒋗 𒉡𒈬𒈾𒁕𒁍𒉈

i18n.en: He could not lie down on a … bedstead; nothing was at his disposal.

notes.official: The disability-litany continues. Umul has no resources, no abilities; *nothing was at his disposal*.

lines.cuneiform: 𒅆𒂍  𒉡𒈬𒈾𒈿 𒉡𒈬𒁕𒀭𒅅𒅅

lines.translit: gub [nu]-mu-da-tuš nu-mu-da-nu2 e2 nu-mu-da-[X] ninda nu-mu-da-[gu7]

i18n.en: He could not stand, nor sit, nor lie down; he could not […] a house; he could not [eat] bread.

notes.official: Final disability-summary: standing, sitting, lying down, house-occupying, bread-eating — all impossible. The five-fold exclusion is total.

lines.cuneiform: 𒁺 𒉡𒈬𒁕𒆪 𒉡𒈬𒁕𒈿 𒂍 𒉡𒈬𒁕 𒃻 𒉡𒈬𒁕𒅥

i18n.en: Ninmah [answered] Enki with a word:

notes.official: Ninmah responds to Enki with the contest-conceding verdict at v 101.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒎏𒂊 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒊏 𒅗𒈠 𒈬𒄄𒄄

lines.translit: lu2 šu dim2-ma-zu lu2 til3-la in-nu lu2 [ug5-ga] /in\-nu il2-bi nu-mu-da

i18n.en: "The being you have fashioned is not a living man, is not a [dead] man — he cannot sustain himself."

notes.official:
**The composition's most-discussed conceptual-category: the *neither-living-nor-dead* liminal-being.** Ninmah's verdict on Umul: *lu2 til3-la in-nu lu2 ug5-ga in-nu* — 'is not a living man, is not a dead man'. The Sumerian-Akkadian liminal-being category is well-attested across the demonological-and-medical corpus (the Akkadian *eṭemmū* ghosts; the *rabiṣu* lurkers; the *mukīl rēš lemutti* bearers-of-evil). Umul belongs to no living-category and no dead-category — Enki's contest-creature is structurally-unprecedented. See overlay entry `lu2-til-la-lu2-ug-ga-neither-living-nor-dead`.

The verdict is the contest's structural-resolution: Ninmah concedes that Enki's creation falls outside any social-role-integration she can devise. The composition's narrator-statement at v 140 will confirm — *Ninmah could not rival the great lord Enki*.

lines.cuneiform: 𒇽 𒋗 𒁶𒈠𒍪 𒇽 𒋾𒆷 𒅔𒉡 𒇽 𒂦𒂵 𒅔𒉡 𒅍𒁉 𒉡𒈬𒁕

i18n.en: Enki answered Ninmah:

notes.official: Enki's response — the destiny-decree recapitulation of vv 103-108.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒀭𒎏𒂊 𒈬𒈾𒉌𒅁𒄄𒄄

lines.translit: lu2 gi šu sig-ra nam mi-ni-tar ninda mi-ni-in-šum2

i18n.en: "To the first one, the man of weak hands, I decreed a destiny — I gave him bread."

notes.official: Enki's recapitulation of the first defective: the weak-handed man (v 59); see overlay entry `lu2-gi-sushuru-sasade-nugam-weak-handed-disabled`. The recapitulation-sequence vv 103-108 is editorially-significant: it emphasizes that *all six* of Ninmah's defectives received destinies-and-bread — the contest is decided not by Enki's failure-of-Ninmah's-creatures (he succeeded with all six) but by Ninmah's inability to find a destiny for Umul.

lines.cuneiform: 𒇽 𒄀 𒋗 𒋝𒊏 𒉆 𒈪𒉌𒋻 𒃻 𒈪𒉌𒅔𒋧

lines.translit: lu2 ĝiš-nu11 gi4-gi4-ra nam mi-ni-tar ninda mi-ni-in-šum2

i18n.en: "To the man who turned back the light I decreed a destiny — I gave him bread."

notes.official: The blind-musician aetiology recapitulated (v 64); see overlay entry `gi-nu-gi-blind-man-marvel-of-onlookers`.

lines.cuneiform: 𒇽 𒄑𒉢 𒄄𒄄𒊏 𒉆 𒈪𒉌𒋻 𒃻 𒈪𒉌𒅔𒋧

lines.translit: /lu2\ ĝiri3 ḫum dab5-ra nam mi-ni-tar ninda mi-ni-in-šum2

i18n.en: "To the man with broken, foot-bound feet I decreed a destiny — I gave him bread."

notes.official: Third defective recapitulated (v 66); the foot-bound man (the main-text reading rather than the *lu2lil* variant).

lines.cuneiform: 𒇽 𒄊  𒆪𒊏 𒉆 𒈪𒉌𒋻 𒃻 𒈪𒉌𒅔𒋧

i18n.en: "To the man dripping [continually with water] I decreed a destiny — [I gave him bread]."

notes.official: Fourth defective recapitulated (v 69); the water-dripping man healed by incantation-water (v 71); see overlay entry `namtar-disease-demon-vs-destiny-parsing-crux`.

lines.cuneiform: 𒇽 𒀀 𒋩𒋩𒊏 𒉆 𒈪𒉌𒋻 𒃻 𒈪𒉌𒅔𒋧

i18n.en: "To the woman who could [not give birth] I decreed a destiny — I [gave her] bread."

notes.official: Fifth defective recapitulated (v 72); the infertile woman established in the women's quarters or set up as a weaver (v 74).

lines.cuneiform: 𒊩 𒉡𒅇𒌅𒊏 𒉆 𒈪𒉌𒋻 𒃻 𒈪𒉌𒅔𒋧

lines.translit: lu2 [su-ba ĝiš3 nu-ĝar gal4-la nu-ĝar]-ra nam mi-ni-[tar ninda mi-ni-in-šum2]

i18n.en: "To the being [whose body had been formed with neither penis nor vulva] I [decreed a destiny — I gave it bread]."

notes.official: Sixth defective recapitulated (v 75); the *tiru* of Nibru; see overlay entries `lu2-su-ba-gish-galla-no-genitalia` and `tiru-third-gender-courtier-palace-attendant`.

lines.cuneiform: 𒇽 𒋢𒁀 𒍑 𒉡𒃻 𒊩𒆷 𒉡𒃻𒊏 𒉆 𒈪𒉌𒋻 𒃻 𒈪𒉌𒅔𒋧

i18n.en: "My sister […]"

notes.official: Enki addresses Ninmah as *nin9-ĝu10* — 'my sister'. The kinship-vocabulary in the divine assembly: Ninmah is variously *Enki's sister* and *the principal birth-goddess*; the kinship-terms reflect the structured-divine-family of the Sumerian pantheon.

lines.cuneiform: 𒎐𒈬

notes.official: Lacuna.
Lacuna.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀀

i18n.en: Nin[mah] [spoke to Enki]:

lines.cuneiform: 𒉌 𒁺  𒋳𒂠 𒈬𒉌𒅔𒆭𒊑

lines.translit: a2-še3 an nu-mu-e-tuš ki nu-[mu-e]-tuš i-bi2 il2-la-zu ka-na-aĝ2-ĝa2 nu-ed2-en

i18n.en: "Now, you do not dwell in heaven, nor [do you] dwell on earth; you, of (such) raised gaze, do not come forth into the Land."

notes.official: **Ninmah's verdict on Umul's existential-exclusion:** he does not dwell in *an* (heaven), does not dwell on *ki* (earth), does not come forth into *ka-na-aĝ2* (the Land = Sumer / the civilized homeland). The three-fold spatial exclusion — heaven, earth, the Land — is total. See central entry `kalam-ka-na-ag-the-land-cross-corpus` for the Sumerian collective-territorial-identity *kalam* lexeme (the Sumerian Land, distinct from *kur* foreign-lands), and the cross-corpus parallel to Hebrew *ha-aretz* (the Land of Israel) and Akkadian *mātu*.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀉𒂠 𒀭 𒉡𒈬𒂊𒆪 𒆠 𒉡𒈬𒂊𒆪 𒄿𒉈 𒅍𒆷𒍪 𒅗𒈾𒉘𒂷 𒉡𒌓𒁺𒂗

lines.translit: ki za-e nu-tuš-en e2-ĝu10 du3-a inim-zu { mu } {() ĝiš} nu-tuku

i18n.en: "The place where you do not dwell — my built house — gives no heed to your word."

notes.official: Ninmah's house pays no heed to Umul's word. Two manuscript variants: { mu } 'name' / {() ĝiš} 'wood, tree, ear'. The reading {() ĝiš} — 'does not have (an) ear (for your word)' — uses the Sumerian wisdom-and-hearing idiom (*ĝiš tuku* — 'to have an ear; to hear; to attend to').

lines.cuneiform: 𒆠 𒍝𒂊 𒉡𒆪𒂗 𒂍𒈬 𒆕𒀀 𒅗𒍪  𒈬   𒄑 𒉡𒌇

lines.translit: ki za-e nu-til3-en iri-ĝu10 du3-a niĝ2-ĝu10 lib ba-sig9-ge-en

i18n.en: "The place where you do not live — my built city — you reduce its things to dread silence."

notes.official: Continuation of Ninmah's verdict. *Iri* — *city* — is the social-civic counterpart of *kalam* (the Land); Ninmah's *built city* is reduced to *lib* — *dread silence* — by Umul's exclusion.

lines.cuneiform: 𒆠 𒍝𒂊 𒉡𒋾𒂗 𒌷𒈬 𒆕𒀀 𒃻𒈬 𒈜 𒁀𒋛𒄀𒂗

lines.translit: [iri]-ĝu10 gel-le-eĝ3-ĝa2 e2-ĝu10 gul-la { du5-mu-> } {() dumu-ĝu10} šu dab5-ba

i18n.en: "My [city] lies in ruin; my house is destroyed; my child has been seized."

notes.official: Ninmah's lament: her city in ruin, her house destroyed, her child seized. The lament register echoes the Sumerian *city-lament* genre (the *Lamentation over the Destruction of Ur*, the *Lamentation over Sumer and Ur*; Black-Cunningham-Robson-Zolyomi ETCSL c.2.2). Two manuscript variants on the child-lexeme: { du5-mu } / {() dumu-ĝu10} — both reading *child* / *son*.

lines.cuneiform: 𒌷𒈬 𒄃𒇷𒉘𒂷 𒂍𒈬 𒄢𒆷  𒂅𒈬   𒌉𒈬 𒋗 𒆪𒁀

i18n.en: "I am a fugitive — driven out from the E-kur!"

notes.official: **Ninmah identifies herself as a fugitive driven out from the E-kur — Enlil's principal temple at Nippur.** The E-kur is the religious-and-political center of the Sumerian world; Ninmah's claim of being driven-out from the E-kur dramatizes her contest-defeat. See central entry `ekur-house-of-the-mountain-enlil-temple-cross-corpus` for the *house of the mountain* etymology and the cross-corpus *temple-as-cosmic-mountain* tradition (Ugaritic Mount Zaphon; Hebrew Bible Mount Zion / *Har ha-Bayit*; Greek Mount Olympus; Vedic Mount Meru).

lines.translit: ud me-e niĝ2-ĝu10 šu-zu-ta šu la-ba-ra-e3

i18n.en: "On that day, what is mine has not slipped from your hand."

notes.official: Ninmah acknowledges that Enki holds the contest in his hand. The contest-resolution is approaching.

lines.cuneiform: 𒌓 𒈨𒂊 𒃻𒈬 𒋗𒍪𒋫 𒋗 𒆷𒁀𒊏𒌓𒁺

i18n.en: Enki answered Ninmah:

notes.official: Speech-introduction; Enki's final speech.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒀭𒎏𒊏 𒈬𒈾𒉌𒅁𒄄𒄄

i18n.en: "The word that has come from your mouth — who can alter it?

notes.official: **The divine *fiat* statement: the word once spoken cannot be altered.** *Inim* (word) and *ka* (mouth) are paired in the canonical Sumerian divine-speech-act-is-irrevocable formula. Cross-corpus to Isa 55:11 (*ken yih'yeh d'vari asher yetze mi-pi lo yashuv elai reiqam* — 'so shall my word be that goes forth from my mouth: it shall not return to me empty') — the irrevocable-divine-word topos is widely-attested across the ANE.

lines.cuneiform: 𒅗 𒅗𒍪 𒌓𒁺𒀀 𒀀𒁀𒀀 𒉌𒉽𒊑

lines.translit: u4-mu-ul X TU dab5-ba ur2-zu-ta šu ĝal2-ab-ta

i18n.en: Take Umul, … … the seized one, from your lap — let your hand be set upon him.

notes.official: Enki places Umul in Ninmah's lap — the maternal-care position. The contest's resolution is *not* the destruction of Umul but his *placement-in-maternal-care* by Ninmah. The resolution is editorially-significant: even the *neither-living-nor-dead* creature receives care, integrated into the divine-family-economy through maternal-tending rather than through bread-and-destiny-decree.

lines.cuneiform: 𒌓𒈬𒌌  𒌅 𒆪𒁀 𒌫𒍪𒋫 𒋗 𒅅𒀊𒋫

lines.translit: ^dnin-maḫ^? kiĝ2-ĝa2-zu ḫe2-bi2-la2-la2 šu nu-du7 ma-dab5 a-ba-am3 saĝ mu-un-ĝa2-ĝa2

i18n.en: Ninmah, may your work be counter-balanced! Imperfect things have seized me — who would set their head upright (= help them)?

notes.official: **Enki's contest-closing declaration: *kiĝ2-ĝa2-zu ḫe2-bi2-la2-la2* — 'may your work be counter-balanced!'** The verb *la2* admits multiple translations: 'undone' (ETCSL); 'matched / counter-balanced' (Jacobsen); 'hang in the balance' (Foster). The WoH adopts the *counter-balance* reading following Jacobsen and the narrative-context. The verb's *la2*-construction at v 57 (Enki's offer to counter-balance Ninmah's destiny) and at v 132 (Enki's contest-closing counter-balance declaration) frames the entire contest as a *matching-and-balancing* enterprise, not a winner-take-all defeat. See overlay entry `la2-line132-ninmah-work-counterbalanced-vs-undone`.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒎏 𒆥𒂷𒍪 𒉈𒇲𒇲 𒋗 𒉡𒌌 𒈠𒆪 𒀀𒁀𒀀𒀭 𒊕 𒈬𒌦𒂷𒂷

lines.translit: lu2 me^?-dim2^?-ĝu10 eĝer-zu-še3 tuku-a ka-bi šu ḫe2-bi2-ĝal2

i18n.en: May the human whose form is mine, who has followed in your wake, set his hand to his mouth (= eat, live).

notes.official: Enki's blessing on humankind. The Sumerian *šu ka ĝar* — 'to set hand to mouth' — is the idiom for *eating, sustaining oneself, living*. The blessing places normal-humanity (whose form is Enki's — *me-dim2-ĝu10*) into the bread-and-living-economy that Umul cannot enter.

lines.cuneiform: 𒇽 𒈬 𒂕𒍪𒂠 𒌇𒀀 𒅗𒁉 𒋗 𒉈𒅅

i18n.en: Today let my potency be praised; may your wisdom of counsel be confirmed!"

notes.official: Enki's contest-closing self-praise — *ĝiš3-ĝu10 me-teš2* — 'may my potency be praised' — and confirmation of Ninmah's wisdom-counsel. The *ĝeštug2 de5-ge* — 'wisdom of counsel' — picks up Ninmah's ability to give and receive counsel; the closing is conciliatory rather than dismissive.

lines.cuneiform: 𒌓𒁕 𒍑𒈬 𒈨𒌨 𒁀𒄿𒄿 𒄑𒌆𒉿 𒊑𒄀𒍪 𒅅

i18n.en: Let the enkum and ninkum (officiants),

notes.official: The *enkum* and *ninkum* are officiant-classes in the Sumerian temple-cult; they are paired here as the cult-personnel who will perform the closing-doxology of the composition.

lines.cuneiform: 𒂗𒉽𒅊𒉣𒈨𒂬 𒎏𒉽𒅊𒉣𒈨𒂬

notes.official: The cult-personnel perform the *foot-prostration* (*ĝiri3 šub-šub*) — the Mesopotamian formal-prostration-of-worship — and praise Enki.

lines.cuneiform: 𒌓  𒄊 𒊒𒊒 𒄘 𒉆𒁉 𒅗 𒋻𒍪 𒋛𒅋𒇷𒉈

i18n.en: "My sister, by the strength of (your) heroism […] …!"

notes.official: Enki addresses Ninmah as *nin9-ĝu10* — 'my sister' (as at v 109) — invoking her *nam-ur-saĝ* (heroism, warrior-strength). The address acknowledges Ninmah's status as a divine-peer.

lines.cuneiform: 𒎐𒈬 𒀉 𒉆𒌨𒊕𒂷  𒁺

i18n.en: Song […] of the scribal art (?) […].

notes.official: *Šir3* — 'song, hymn' — and *nam-dub* — 'the scribal art / the office of the tablet-writer'. The reference may be to the composition itself as a song-of-the-scribal-art, performed in the temple-school context.

lines.cuneiform: 𒂡  𒉆

lines.translit: diĝir ĝiš tuku-a-bi u4-mu-ul du3^? […] e2-ĝu10 ḫe2-ak-[e]

i18n.en: "The gods who heard this — let Umul build (?) […] and act on my behalf in my house!"

notes.official: Enki's final disposition for Umul: assigned to *build / act / function* in Enki's house. Even the *neither-living-nor-dead* creature receives a divine-assigned-role — in Enki's own domestic-economy. The closure is editorially-significant: no creature is wasted in the Sumerian creation-economy; all are placed.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭 𒄑 𒌇𒀀𒁉 𒌓𒈬𒌌   𒂍𒈬 𒀝𒂊

i18n.en: Ninmah could not rival the great lord Enki.

notes.official: **The narrator's contest-resolution statement.** *Zag nu-mu-ni-in-ša4* — 'she did not rival him at the side'. The contest is decided in favor of Enki; Ninmah cannot match Umul. The resolution is final and is the composition's narrative-pivot toward the closing-doxology of v 141.

lines.cuneiform: 𒀭𒎏𒂊 𒂗 𒃲 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 𒍠 𒉡𒈬𒉌𒅔𒁺

i18n.en: O father Enki, sweet is your praise!

notes.official: **The composition's doxological-closing formula.** *Za3-mi2* — *praise* — is the foundational Sumerian doxological-praise lexeme, deployed in the canonical closing-formula of many Sumerian compositions: *a-a [Divine-Name] za3-mi2-zu dug3-ga* — 'O father / lord [Divine-Name], sweet is your praise'. The formula closes most of the Enki-cycle compositions (*Enki and the World Order*, *Enki and Ninhursaĝa*, *Inana and Enki*), the Inana-cycle compositions, several of the temple-hymns, and various cult-poems. See central entry `za-mi-doxological-praise-formula-sumerian-cross-corpus` for the cross-corpus parallels to Akkadian *tanattu* and Hebrew *tehillah / hallel / barukh*. The 'sweet is your praise' (*dug3-ga*) epithet parallels Hebrew *naim* (Ps 135:3, 147:1). The DINGIR-determinative ^d is preserved in the translit field; the divine-name *Enki* without prefix in the prose per the overlay convention `dingir-prefix-prose-drop-convention`.
